answers.text: The brief does not say how on-call starts a rollback (CLI command, button or ticket). The document now says on-call sends a rollback request to the rollout controller, and that the controller is the only writer of billing_mode. The mechanism is listed as an open question.

A human asks the controller to move a mode. The controller reads its own gate record and checks that gate. shadow to both needs a 7-day streak under 0.1 percent with at least 5,000 invoices compared in the window. both to new_only needs 14 days in both, no unresolved mismatches and Finance sign-off present. If all checks pass, the controller writes billing_mode and the gate record in one versioned transaction. If a check fails, it refuses and records the reason. The document now states this under Human moves and gate checks. Who may sign off is open.

The brief does not say who computes the automatic 2 percent trigger or from what data, and it gives no minimum charge count per 10-minute window. A proposal (the new engine emits each charge outcome and the controller computes the rate per window) is written in the document as an open question, not as settled design.

Finance sign-off is a field in the controller's gate record, set by a human action in the controller and cleared when withdrawn. The document says the gate record holds it and that withdrawal clears the field. The brief does not say who is authorised to sign off. That is listed as open.

billing_mode keeps its pre-rollback value until hand off. A rollback_in_progress flag in the gate record tells the new engine to stop charging before each charge. In both, the old engine does not charge, so during freeze and drain nobody charges and due periods wait. In shadow, the old engine has been charging throughout, so the freeze is a no-op. The document now says this under Rollback.

From shadow, the new engine never charged, so steps 1 and 2 only confirm that no new-engine charge is in flight. The old engine charged throughout, so charging continues. Step 3 confirms the ledger. Shadow invoices and comparison output are kept for audit, not written to the ledger, and not deleted. The document now has a per-source-mode note under Rollback.

The ledger is the system of record. A customer-period is settled when the ledger holds a provider-confirmed charge for it, with the provider idempotency key. Whichever engine charges writes that entry. The reconcile step confirms and marks entries for every period either engine charged. Both engines check the ledger before charging. The brief does not define the ledger schema, so the exact marker is an open question.

The Halted to Freeze edge was wrong. It now has one resume edge to each step, labelled as the on-call resume of that failed step, and the controller records the failed step. Hand_off_to_old_engine now has a failure edge to Halted, and the failure section says a failed hand off leaves billing_mode unchanged and halts.

The brief does not say who writes the usage event log. It does give the 35-day retention. The document says the old engine, in new_only, does not compute from the events, so the events stay in the log. Catch-up reads the retained events from the start of new_only and writes their invoices to the ledger, skipping periods already settled. Writer and exact retention behaviour are open.

The brief does not say what happens to a rollback that is in progress or Halted on day 35. The document now says the day-35 closure fires only from new_only with no rollback in progress. Charging stays paused and nothing returns to old_only until a person decides. Whether an earlier rollback may finish catch-up after day 35 is open.

answers.text: The brief's gate is a rate: each day's mismatch rate must be under 0.1 percent, so a day with some mismatches can count. The rate decides, not the presence of a mismatch. My earlier sentence that any mismatch resets the streak was my own invention and is removed. The document now defines mismatch, mismatch rate and a counted day under Daily comparison. On a day with 1,000 or fewer invoices, any mismatch fails the day.

The controller computes the counters. The nightly job writes one result per date (date, invoices compared, mismatches, complete or not) and nothing else. The controller reads each date once and updates the gate record, keyed by date, so a re-run does not double-count. Reason: the controller is the only writer of the gate record, so it keeps the record consistent with billing_mode. Days in both are computed from both_entered_at, so no counter is kept for them.

From shadow, the old engine is not paused. It is the only charger throughout, and billing_mode stays shadow until hand off. A single charging rule now states this: the old engine charges when billing_mode is old_only or shadow, and the new engine when billing_mode is both or new_only with no rollback flag set. A Halted rollback from shadow leaves the old engine charging. From both or new_only, neither engine charges until hand off, so due periods wait. The old blanket statement that charging stays paused has been replaced.

Catch-up writes invoices to the ledger only and charges nothing. billing_mode is new_only during catch-up, so under the charging rule the old engine does not charge then. Periods that came due during the rollback wait until hand off. After hand off, billing_mode is old_only, and the old engine charges the unsettled due periods, skipping settled ones. Reason: billing_mode is the single switch that says who charges, and only one engine may charge at a time.

The controller stores new_only_entered_at in the same change that sets billing_mode to new_only. Day 35 is 35 times 24 hours after that time, in UTC. Rollback requests are refused by comparing the current time with that entry time when the request arrives, so a missed daily check cannot reopen rollback. The daily check only sets new_only_closed in the gate record. Reason: the retention limit is a fixed time, so eligibility should not depend on a timer.

Only one rollback runs at a time. A start request is accepted only from shadow, both or new_only with no rollback active. A resume request is accepted only while Halted and resumes at the recorded step. Any other on-call request, any automatic trigger, and any human move made while a rollback is running or Halted is refused or ignored, and the reason is recorded. Reason: the steps share one rollback_in_progress flag and one recorded step, so two concurrent runs could both attempt hand off.

questions.text: Which component actually executes each rollback step: the rollout controller itself, the engines, or on-call? If the controller crashes mid-step, how does it know where to continue?

questions.text: The doc says hand off and human moves are one versioned change, but also that no transaction spans the config service and the gate record. Which statement holds today? What state do workers see if only one of the two writes lands?
questions.about: Hand off: as one versioned change / Open questions: billing_mode and gate record in separate stores

questions.text: After the provider reports the outcome of an in-flight charge (charged, not charged, or still unknown), what is written to the ledger for each? If the provider never answers, does the step wait, fail to Halted, or time out?
questions.about: Drain_in_flight: resolved against the provider by idempotency key

questions.text: What does the old engine do in catch-up mode for periods that the new engine already computed but did not charge? Is it a full recompute from the events, and how is it triggered and finished?

questions.about: Gate record unreadable

questions.text: What stops two charges for the same customer-period if the ledger check and the charge are not atomic, such as at the mode switch after hand off? Is the provider idempotency key the final protection, and how is the key made?
questions.about: Both engines check the ledger for a settled entry before each charge

answers.text: The rollout controller executes every rollback step. It sets and clears the flags, queries the provider during drain, writes the ledger, runs the old engine in catch-up mode during step 4, and makes the hand-off writes. The engines only charge as the charging rule allows. Before each step the controller writes rollback_step to the gate record, and it records completion before moving on. After a crash, a restarted controller reads rollback_status and rollback_step and reruns the recorded step. Steps are idempotent, so a crash between finishing a step and recording it is safe. Reason: the controller is the only writer of the gate record. Open: how step 1 learns that no charge is in flight outside the intent rows.

The statement 'one versioned change' was wrong. No transaction spans the config service and the gate record, so the document now defines a fixed write order. A forward move writes the gate record first (pending_mode, plus both_entered_at or new_only_entered_at), then billing_mode in the config service, then clears pending_mode. Hand off writes billing_mode = old_only first, then clears rollback_in_progress, resets the gates and clears the sign-off. Workers' view after a partial write: if only a forward move's first write has landed, billing_mode is still the old mode, and each mode has exactly one charger. If only hand off's first write has landed, rollback_in_progress is still set, so the new engine stays stopped, and the old engine may charge because steps 1 to 4 have finished. A restarted controller completes whatever is pending. This is designed but not tested. Unknown: whether the config service supports a compare-and-set or versioned write.

Charged: write a settled ledger entry for the customer-period with the key and the provider's confirmation. Not charged (the provider confirms no charge exists for that key): clear the intent row, so the period is due again and can be charged later with the same key. Unknown: the intent row stays pending, which blocks both engines from charging that customer-period. The drain step waits and halts with the key in rollback_last_error if no answer arrives by a timeout. The timeout length is not given, so it is unknown. An unknown outcome is never re-sent on a guess.

Periods the new engine computed in new_only already have ledger invoices, because the new engine writes the ledger in new_only, so catch-up does not replace them. Catch-up is a full recompute from usage events since new_only_entered_at, in event order, to rebuild the old engine's state. For each customer-period: if it is settled, skip it; if the ledger holds an unsettled invoice, keep that invoice and record any difference for review; if the ledger holds no invoice, write one as due. It charges nothing. The controller triggers it as step 4, only from new_only, saves its position as catch_up_cursor, and finishes when every event since entry is processed. Reason for not overwriting: a ledger invoice may already be the basis of a due charge, so changing it changes what is billed. Open: whether differences should block hand off (the document says they do not), and what happens if events expire before catch-up ends.

The comparison covers customer-periods whose billing period ends on that UTC date, for both engines' outputs. Invoices generated that day are not used, because one period's invoice could be produced over several days and be compared partly. A comparison is complete when both engines finished and produced output for every customer-period with usage events for a period ending that day. Anything else is incomplete. The time zone is UTC. The brief does not define billing periods, so the period boundaries are an assumption and are listed as open.

The controller cannot write the gate record, so it refuses state-changing requests and cannot run steps until the record is readable. It retries. The new engine does not charge, because it cannot confirm that no rollback is in progress. The old engine does not depend on the gate record. Its charging rule reads billing_mode alone, so in shadow it keeps charging. In both and new_only the old engine does not charge, so during a gate outage nothing charges in those modes. Whether that is acceptable is open.

A read-then-charge check is not atomic, so the document now uses an intent row. Before calling the provider, an engine makes a conditional insert in the ledger for the customer-period, keyed by customer ID and billing period ID. Only the engine whose insert succeeds may charge. The idempotency key is derived from customer ID and billing period ID alone, with no engine name, attempt number or amount, so every attempt from either engine sends the same key. The provider's idempotency key is the second line of protection. Unknown: whether the provider honours a repeated key across engines, and how it treats a different amount under the same key. The conditional insert also needs a unique constraint on the ledger, which the brief does not confirm.

questions.text: What starts an automatic rollback in the controller: does something send it a request like on-call does, and what does it record as rollback_source for automatic versus on-call starts?
questions.about: Automatic rollback: new-engine charge failure rate above 2 percent in a 10-minute window

answers.text: old_only to shadow uses the same commit order as the other forward moves. Step 1, gate record: set pending_mode to shadow, set shadow_streak_days and shadow_streak_invoices to zero, and record shadow_started_at. Step 2, config service: set billing_mode to shadow. Step 3, gate record: clear pending_mode. No gate is checked. The document now states this in Commit order. Reason: every mode change should use one recovery path, and the streak must start at zero before the new engine begins writing shadow output.

The controller does not search the ledger for charges that lack a settled entry. The new engine and the old engine each insert a conditional intent row before any provider call, so every charge that may have happened has an intent row carrying its idempotency key. The set of charged customer-periods is therefore the set of intent rows. Step 2 asks the provider about each key. Step 3 then verifies that no intent row is pending and writes a settled entry for any charged key whose settlement write failed. The provider's answer format for a key (charge reference, amount, and how it reports unknown) is not in the brief and is listed as open.

The check happens after the intent-row insert. An engine first inserts its intent row, then reads rollback_in_progress from the gate record, and charges only if the flag is clear and the record is readable. If the flag is set, the engine leaves the intent row, and drain clears it as not charged. This order means that any engine which read the flag as clear had already written its row, so the controller's scan after setting the flag sees it. Step 1 completes on that scan, with no worker acknowledgement or fixed wait. The argument assumes the flag and the intent rows are read in a consistent order, which the brief does not confirm, so it is listed as open.

The nightly job writes two things per UTC date: one count row (date, invoices compared, mismatches, complete or not) and one mismatch record per mismatched customer-period, with both totals and an open or resolved status. The earlier rule that it writes nothing else was wrong, because the 14-day gate could not be read from counts alone. The 14-day gate counts open mismatch records since both_entered_at. A date re-run replaces its own rows. What marks a record resolved, who may mark it, and how a mismatch in a ledger invoice that has already been charged gets resolved are not defined in the brief, so they stay open.

When hand off fails after its first write, billing_mode is old_only and rollback_in_progress is still set. The old engine charges under its own rule, because billing_mode alone allows it, and this is intended because steps 1 to 4 have finished and the new engine is blocked by the flag. On-call resume runs hand off again. Both writes are idempotent, so the rerun is safe. Forward moves, new rollback starts, automatic triggers and any resume other than hand off are refused during this window, and each refusal is recorded. The document now spells this out under Hand off after its first write.

No separate request is sent. The controller evaluates the automatic trigger itself, from new-engine charge outcomes it reads, and it applies the same start rules as an on-call request. rollback_source is recorded as on_call with the requester for on-call starts, and as automatic:charge_failure_rate for automatic starts. The data source and the window rule for the rate are still open, as the earlier open question already says.

questions.about: Charge intent: The intent row becomes settled when the provider confirms the charge

questions.text: After drain clears an intent row as not charged, can a late call from the new engine, which already read the flag clear, still reach the provider with the same key? How is that handled?
questions.about: Drain_in_flight: Not charged, clear the intent row

answers.text: The engine that made the charge writes the settled entry itself, straight after the provider confirms, with the key and the confirmation. If that write fails after the charge succeeded, the row stays pending (it is not cleared, because the charge may have happened). The engine retries the write. A pending row blocks both engines from charging that customer-period, so the failure stalls the period but cannot cause a second charge. If the engine cannot finish, the controller resolves the row by key with the drain rules. The document now says this under Charge intent. How often the controller runs that resolution outside a rollback, and its timeout, are open.

The brief does not say what makes a customer-period due, what starts an engine's charge attempt (schedule, event or polling loop), or where the workers run. The document now defines due as a ledger invoice with no settled entry, which the catch-up rule already relies on. The trigger and the worker location are listed as open questions.

The brief does not give how often workers read billing_mode, whether they cache it, or how stale it can be. The document does not depend on these for no double charge: the intent row stops a second charge to the same customer-period whichever engine reads a stale mode. A stale read can still let the wrong engine charge in a mode, so that is now listed under what happens when something fails. The staleness bound is open.

Yes. A day that does not count sets shadow_streak_days and shadow_streak_invoices to zero together. The 5,000-invoice total is counted over the same consecutive run as the 7-day streak, so invoices from a broken run must not carry over. The document now says so under Daily comparison and in the Assumptions. The brief does not state this; it is my design decision.

The brief does not say what runs the nightly job or when it runs, so the schedule is open. For readiness, the job writes mismatch records first and the count row last. The controller reads only dates that have a count row, so a count row means its mismatch records exist. The document now says this under Daily comparison.

The unsettled ledger invoice. After hand off, the old engine charges the amount of the ledger invoice for an unsettled period and does not recompute and overwrite it. In both, the new engine's invoice is the one in the ledger, and the ledger is the system of record. This is the same rule catch-up uses, so an unsettled ledger invoice is never overwritten by either engine. The old engine's shadow-store total is not used for charging. Reason: a second total for the same period could bill a different amount. The document now states this under Charge intent.

This was a real gap. The new engine can read the flag as clear, insert its row, and send the charge after drain has already asked the provider and been told no charge exists. The provider's idempotency key does not stop a first request that arrives late. The document now says drain may clear a row as not charged only after a charge deadline has passed since the row was inserted, and that an engine must not send a provider call for a row older than that deadline. The deadline length, and whether the provider's answer is final after it, are not known and are listed as open questions.

questions.text: If a forward move is pending (pending_mode set, config write maybe landed) and on-call or the automatic trigger asks for a rollback, is it accepted or refused? Which mode counts as the rollback source then?
questions.about: Rollback start / pending_mode

questions.text: If the provider says no charge exists but the intent row is younger than the charge deadline, what does drain do? Does it wait and ask again, and who tracks that wait?
questions.about: Drain_in_flight: Not charged

questions.text: What does the scan read, and how does the controller know it has found every row? Is it one query over the ledger for all unsettled intent rows, and what if an engine inserts another row after the scan, then reads the flag as set?
questions.about: Freeze_new_charges: scanned the intent rows after that write and found every row

questions.text: What happens to the old engine's intent rows in a rollback from shadow or both? The old engine does not read the gate flag, so how are its in-flight rows stopped or handled in steps 1 and 2?
questions.about: Intent row insert / Insert the intent row

answers.text: A rollback request or automatic trigger that arrives while pending_mode is set is held until the pending move completes. The controller first completes the pending move (steps 2 and 3 of the forward move, with no gate recheck, because its checks already passed), then records the rollback start with rollback_from_mode set to the mode it completed to. Reason: on-call can start a rollback at any time, and refusing would leave a failing rollout running. Exposure: after the pending move completes and before the rollback flag is set, the new engine may charge if the target is both or new_only. Any such charge has an intent row, which drain resolves. Whether to accept that exposure is listed as open.

Drain does not clear a not-charged row that is younger than the charge deadline. The row stays pending, which blocks both engines from that customer-period, and drain asks the provider again on a later pass. The controller tracks the wait: rollback_step stays at drain, and the wait is measured from the insert timestamp recorded in the ledger, so a restart resumes it. The row is cleared only when the provider says no charge exists and the deadline has passed. The pass interval, the deadline length and the provider latency bound are open. The wait is bounded by the same timeout as an unknown answer, which is also open.

The scan is one ledger query for unsettled intent rows inserted by the new engine, and it runs after the flag write. Completeness relies on ordering, not on a count: a new-engine worker that read the flag as clear had already inserted its row before that read, so a query after the flag write sees it. A worker that reads the flag as set may insert a row after the query. It does not charge, and step 2 repeats the query until none remain. To stop frozen workers from creating rows at all, the new engine now also reads the flag before inserting. Whether the ledger query sees an insert that completed before the flag read is open, because the brief does not confirm consistency across the two stores.

A rollback from shadow does not stop the old engine. It charges in shadow and in old_only alike, so the rollback does not change who charges, and its intent rows follow its normal settle path. Steps 1 to 3 cover only new-engine intent rows, because only the new engine has a flag check and is frozen. Every intent row now records the engine that inserted it, as metadata outside the key. In both and new_only the old engine does not charge, so it creates no rows there. Old-engine rows left pending from an earlier shadow phase are outside steps 1 to 3. They still block their customer-period, and the normal controller resolution handles them.
